articles.title: Prepare before visiting a hospital
articles.summary: Contact the facility and confirm the service you need.
articles.content: Check the hospital address, telephone number, listed department, and operating information. Call first for clinic schedules, referrals, cost information, required documents, and whether specialist or laboratory services are available. Bring identification, previous records, medicine names, and a contact person. For immediate danger, use an emergency unit or local emergency service rather than waiting for a routine clinic.

articles.title: Recognize warning signs and act promptly
articles.summary: Emergency care is for severe, rapidly worsening, or life-threatening conditions.
articles.content: Difficulty breathing, severe bleeding, collapse, chest pain, stroke-like weakness or facial droop, severe head injury, convulsions, suspected poisoning, and serious allergic reactions require immediate emergency help. Do not move a person unnecessarily after major trauma. Call the facility or emergency service, give a clear location and condition, and follow their instructions. This guide cannot replace emergency dispatch or clinical assessment.

articles.title: Reduce common infection risks
articles.summary: Simple habits help protect households and communities.
articles.content: Wash hands with soap and clean water after using a toilet and before preparing or eating food. Use safe drinking water, cook food thoroughly, cover or store food safely, and ventilate crowded rooms. Use local mosquito and water-safety guidance. Stay away from others while seriously unwell if advised, and seek medical advice for persistent fever, cough, diarrhea, or worsening symptoms.

articles.title: Keep an immunization record up to date
articles.summary: Vaccines protect children and some adults.
articles.content: Vaccines are offered according to Uganda’s public immunization schedule. Keep a child health card and take it to each visit so due vaccines are not missed. Vaccines may cause short-lived redness, fever, or soreness. Severe breathing difficulty, swelling of the face or throat, or collapse after vaccination is an emergency and needs immediate care. Ask a health worker about missed doses and adult vaccination where applicable.

articles.title: Build a varied everyday meal
articles.summary: Choose accessible foods across the main food groups.
articles.content: A balanced meal can include a starchy staple, a protein food such as beans, eggs, fish, or meat, fruits or vegetables, and clean water. Add variety when affordable rather than relying on one type of food. Infants have specific feeding needs; ask a health worker or caregiver-support service for advice. Seek assessment for persistent poor growth, severe weight loss, unusual swelling, or feeding difficulty.

articles.title: Know your options for HIV testing and prevention
articles.summary: Confidential services help people make informed decisions.
articles.content: Free or low-cost HIV testing and counseling are available through many Ugandan public health facilities. Ask a health worker about testing, condoms, HIV prevention medicines, treatment, pregnancy planning, and confidential reproductive care. HIV treatment works best when started early and taken consistently. A positive or negative result should be explained privately, with follow-up and partner support when appropriate.

articles.title: Prevent malaria and seek testing early
articles.summary: Practical prevention and when to test.
articles.content: Use insecticide-treated bed nets, keep mosquito control measures around living areas, and follow locally recommended prevention advice. Fever can have several causes, so malaria should be confirmed with a rapid test or microscopy before treatment whenever possible. Do not give leftover medicine or share another person’s prescription. A person who has severe weakness, confusion, breathing difficulty, convulsions, persistent vomiting, or cannot drink needs urgent medical attention.

articles.title: Know when a sick child needs urgent care
articles.summary: Use a calm checklist of urgent warning signs.
articles.content: A child who is difficult to wake, unable to drink, breathing unusually fast or with difficulty, having convulsions, becoming unusually floppy or irritable, or looking much worse should receive urgent medical assessment. Fever, cough, diarrhea, and vomiting can become serious when a child has poor feeding or dehydration. Follow advice from a qualified health worker and do not delay care because a clinic is closed. Seek the nearest appropriate emergency or pediatric service.

articles.title: Prepare for antenatal and delivery care
articles.summary: What to ask and arrange before and during pregnancy.
articles.content: Antenatal care provides regular checks on the health of the pregnant person and baby. If possible, begin antenatal visits early and attend all recommended appointments. Keep a record of visits, medicines, allergies, and expected delivery date. Seek immediate help for severe bleeding, severe headache, vision changes, convulsions, severe abdominal pain, difficulty breathing, or reduced baby movement after quickening. These are warning signs, not normal discomfort; contact a health facility or emergency service promptly.
